title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
content:
# Atomic Number and Mass Number

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Define atomic number and mass number
- Use atomic notation to represent atoms
- Calculate the number of subatomic particles from atomic notation
- Understand why atomic number determines the element

## Introduction

Every atom can be uniquely described using two numbers: the **atomic number** and the **mass number**. These numbers tell us the composition of the atom and identify which element it is.

## Key Concepts

### Atomic Number (Z)

The **atomic number** is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

$$Z = \text{Number of protons}$$

**Key facts:**
- Every element has a unique atomic number
- The atomic number defines the element (e.g., all atoms with 6 protons are carbon)
- In a neutral atom, atomic number also equals the number of electrons
- Atomic number is also called the **proton number**
- Elements in the Periodic Table are arranged by increasing atomic number

### Mass Number (A)

The **mass number** is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

$$A = \text{Number of protons} + \text{Number of neutrons}$$

or

$$A = Z + N$$

where N = number of neutrons.

**Key facts:**
- Mass number is always a whole number
- Mass number gives the approximate relative atomic mass
- Different atoms of the same element can have different mass numbers (isotopes)

### Calculating Neutrons

To find the number of neutrons:

$$\text{Number of neutrons} = A - Z$$

$$\text{Number of neutrons} = \text{Mass number} - \text{Atomic number}$$

### Atomic Notation

Atoms are represented using **atomic notation** (also called nuclide notation):

$$^A_Z X$$

Where:
- X = Chemical symbol of the element
- A = Mass number (top)
- Z = Atomic number (bottom)

**Examples:**
- $^{12}_6\text{C}$ - Carbon with 6 protons and 6 neutrons
- $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}$ - Sodium with 11 protons and 12 neutrons
- $^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}$ - Chlorine with 17 protons and 18 neutrons

[DIAGRAM: Atomic notation showing position of mass number and atomic number]

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** An atom is represented as $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}$. Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in this atom.

**Solution:**
- Atomic number (Z) = 13, so protons = 13
- Electrons = 13 (neutral atom)
- Neutrons = A - Z = 27 - 13 = 14

**Answer:** 13 protons, 14 neutrons, 13 electrons

**Example 2:** Write the atomic notation for an atom of potassium with 19 protons and 20 neutrons.

**Solution:**
- Element symbol = K (potassium)
- Atomic number (Z) = 19
- Mass number (A) = 19 + 20 = 39

**Answer:** $^{39}_{19}\text{K}$

**Example 3:** Two atoms are represented as $^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}$. Explain why they are both chlorine atoms.

**Solution:** Both atoms have an atomic number of 17, meaning they both have 17 protons. Since the atomic number (number of protons) defines the element, both are chlorine atoms. They have different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons.

## Why Atomic Number Defines the Element

| Atomic Number | Element | Protons |
|---------------|---------|--------|
| 1 | Hydrogen | 1 |
| 6 | Carbon | 6 |
| 8 | Oxygen | 8 |
| 11 | Sodium | 11 |
| 26 | Iron | 26 |
| 79 | Gold | 79 |

If you change the number of protons, you change the element. This can only happen in nuclear reactions, not chemical reactions.

## Exam Tips

- The atomic number is always the smaller number
- Remember: **Z** for atomic number (think 'Z' comes before 'A' in the alphabet, and the atomic number is smaller)
- Always check your calculation: protons + neutrons = mass number

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Confusing atomic number and mass number positions in notation
- **Correct:** Mass number is always on top, atomic number is on the bottom

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to subtract when finding neutrons
- **Correct:** Neutrons = Mass number - Atomic number

- **Mistake:** Thinking atomic number can change
- **Correct:** Atomic number defines the element and doesn't change in chemical reactions

## Practice Questions

1. Define the term 'atomic number'. (1 mark)

2. An atom of nitrogen is represented as $^{14}_{7}\text{N}$. State the number of:
   a) Protons (1 mark)
   b) Neutrons (1 mark)
   c) Electrons (1 mark)

3. Write the atomic notation for an atom of calcium (Ca) with 20 protons and 20 neutrons. (2 marks)

4. Explain why atoms of $^{63}_{29}\text{Cu}$ and $^{65}_{29}\text{Cu}$ are both copper atoms, even though they have different mass numbers. (3 marks)

5. An atom has 12 protons, 12 neutrons, and 12 electrons.
   a) Write the atomic notation for this atom. (2 marks)
   b) Name the element. (1 mark)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Atomic number (Z) | The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom |
| Mass number (A) | The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus |
| Proton number | Another name for atomic number |
| Nucleon number | Another name for mass number |
| Atomic notation | A way of representing atoms showing mass number and atomic number |

## Summary

- Atomic number (Z) = number of protons; defines the element
- Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons
- Number of neutrons = A - Z
- Atomic notation: $^A_Z X$ (mass number on top, atomic number below)
- Elements in the Periodic Table are arranged by increasing atomic number
